text.p: British retailer Laura Ashley reported a 70 percent jump in profits Tuesday and announced plans to expand home furnishings as part of a radical shake-up under its new American chief executive, Ann Iverson.
But the profit recovery failed to match expectations and the retailer's shares fell steeply, off 22 pence at 192 pence at midday.

Pretax profits rose to 5.2 million pounds ($8.1 million) from three million ($6.7 million). Sales fell to 156 million pounds ($243 million) from 164.6 million ($256 million) because of a reduction in mail order and perfume activities and the sale of the company's Australian operations last year.
Industry analysts were unimpressed with the latest performance. "The market had expected profits of six million pounds ($9.3 million) and a dividend of 0.5 pence," said one.

Laura Ashley, famous for its traditionally English flowery dresses and furnishings, has begun expanding its higher-margin home furnishings business in Britain and the United States as part of a three-year recovery programme.
Chief Executive Ann Iverson, who took over last year, said the company's recovery was running to plan.

"The group remains on track through its shop expansion programme and its focus on improving product and gross margins, to achieve acceptable returns for shareholders over the next three years," she said in a statement.

Iverson, who made her name in Britain by turning around Storehouse Plc's BhS and childrenswear chain Mothercare, was hired last year to revive profits as Laura Ashley was struggling to cope with financial troubles caused by over-expansion and under-investment.
The retailer is in the process of closing smaller shops and opening larger ones to display its home furnishing goods, which have scope for bigger profits.
It plans to add more than 100,000 square feet of store space in the United States this year mainly via larger format stores, finance director Jim Walsh said in an interview.
In Britain, Laura Ashley is adding 33,000 square feet of space this year, opening 16 new stores and closing six.
The group also plans to expand its presence in supermarket group Sainsbury's Homebase stores, where it currently has 65 outlets, Walsh said.

He denied that the new-look fashions and fabrics would move completely away from the Laura Ashley floral prints, which turned the business from a cottage industry in the 1950s into an international brand.
"It's taking the flower and updating it," Walsh said.
